claims.text: Restricted atomic mobility in the initial solid state primarily governs the premelting and melting behavior of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Statistical dilution of each element in the multicomponent solid solution governs the nanoparticles' premelting and melting behavior.
Restricted mobility and elemental dilution kinetically delay melting relative to single-metal or binary nanoparticles.
Restricted mobility and elemental dilution produce spatially heterogeneous melting and an extended premelting regime.
The initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are chemically homogeneous.
The nanoparticles possess inherent lattice strains.
A solid precursor state limits free atomic mobility.
A larger number of component elements promotes a more random alloy configuration when free atomic mobility is limited.
Localized heterogeneities and defect sites act as nucleation centers for molten regions.
Individual-element concentrations are lower in a multicomponent system.
Melting onset requires localized atomic rearrangements because mobility is kinetically hindered in the solid precursor.
The nanoparticle melts through multiple spatially separated nucleation sites.
Multiple spatially separated melting sites extend the premelting regime relative to simpler nanoparticles.
Under identical heating conditions, Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will show a delayed overall melting onset relative to size- and morphology-matched monometallic or binary nanoparticles.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will display localized molten regions during premelting.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will exhibit altered latent-heat patterns relative to monometallic or binary controls.
The proposed mechanism applies to nanoparticles produced from solid precursors with limited free atomic mobility.
The mechanism may not apply to solution-phase processing that permits substantially greater species mobility.
A controlled test should compare Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu and binary nanoparticles of similar size and morphology under the same rapid heating ramp.
Failure to observe a statistically significant melting delay, extended premelting regime, or localized molten regions relative to the binary control would falsify the hypothesis.
